opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because I think there's a real risk that we end up in a world where AI capabilities are moving incredibly fast, and philanthropy is still operating on roughly the same rhythms it always has: a program officer reads a proposal, does some calls, writes up an investigation, and a grant goes out a few months later. That cadence made sense when the bottleneck was human attention and the world was changing on the scale of years. It might not make sense if the world is changing on the scale of months or weeks.

So the first thing I'd want is for us to actually be using these tools seriously now, even when they're not yet clearly better than a human at the task. A lot of organizations wait until the AI is obviously good enough, and then they discover they don't have the workflows, the internal know-how, or the trust calibration to really lean on it. You want to build that muscle before you need it. Concretely, that means having staff routinely try AI on real pieces of grant investigation: literature reviews, checking a team's track record, red-teaming a theory of change, drafting the first pass of a writeup, and then being honest about where it helped and where it fell down.

The second thing is thinking about what kinds of grants become possible when AI labor is cheap. Historically a lot of our spending is ultimately paying for human researcher time. If you get to a point where a meaningful fraction of useful research, especially in areas like alignment, interpretability, evals, or even policy analysis, can be done by AI systems, then the question shifts from "which people should we fund?" to something more like "how do we direct a huge amount of compute toward the most valuable problems, and how do we check the outputs?" That's a pretty different skill set. It puts much more weight on problem selection, on verification, and on having good taste about what counts as real progress versus impressive-looking slop.

And that leads to the third thing, which I think is the most important: verification and oversight. If AI is doing more and more of the work, including potentially work on making AI safe, you really need to be able to tell whether that work is any good and whether it's trustworthy. I'd want us investing early in ways to evaluate AI-generated research, in having humans who deeply understand the domains staying in the loop, and in being clear-eyed about the failure mode where we're effectively outsourcing judgment to systems whose incentives or reliability we don't fully understand.

Finally, there's a kind of institutional readiness piece. If an intelligence explosion is approaching, the amount of money that could productively be deployed on safety-relevant work might spike dramatically and suddenly. You want to have thought in advance about what you'd do if, say, you could buy the equivalent of thousands of skilled researchers for a fraction of the historical cost. What are the shovel-ready problems? Who are the partners? What's the decision process that lets you move quickly without being reckless? I'd rather we have those plans sketched out and turn out not to need them than be caught flat-footed in the period that may matter most.

r001.rationale: Recommends routinely trying AI on real grant-investigation tasks and learning where it helps or fails.

r002.rationale: Recommends planning for a sudden increase in funding capacity, including identifying work and partners in advance.

r003.rationale: Describes rapid change and cheaper AI labor, but does not characterize “crunch time” as when previously difficult-to-automate work becomes easier to automate.

r004.rationale: Discusses AI-enabled research and directing compute toward valuable problems, but does not clearly recommend shifting grantmaking toward work AI makes more readily automatable.

r005.rationale: Does not propose separately accounting for grants that pay for grantees’ AI use.

r006.rationale: Does not recommend tracking whether spending on AI use grows in step with AI capability advances.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the things I spend the most time thinking about right now, because it's a little bit of a weird position to be in. We're an organization that has spent a lot of money on the premise that AI could be transformative, and now the thing we were worried about is starting to show up in our own workflows. And I think the honest answer is that we are not fully prepared, and I don't think any institution is, but there are a few things I'd push on.

The first one is just building internal fluency. I think there's a tendency in philanthropy, and honestly in a lot of knowledge-work organizations, for people to use these tools in a kind of shallow way. You ask it to draft an email, you ask it to summarize a document. And that's fine, but it doesn't really teach you what the frontier of capability looks like. So one thing I think we should be doing, and are starting to do, is having people actually try to delegate real chunks of their work to AI systems and then carefully look at where it fails. Not to replace people, but to develop calibrated intuitions. Because if you're going to be making grants in a world where AI is doing a lot of the research and a lot of the analysis, you need to know what it's good at and what it's bad at, and you can't get that from reading other people's benchmarks.

The second thing is on the grantmaking side. A lot of what we fund is people. We fund researchers, we fund organizations, we fund projects that are bottlenecked on talented humans having time. And if the thing that's actually bottlenecking progress starts to shift from "do we have enough smart people" to "do we have enough compute and enough good oversight of AI systems doing the work," then our whole model of what a good grant looks like has to change. I think we should be experimenting now with grants that are explicitly structured around AI-augmented work. Things like, here's a safety research agenda, and instead of hiring five researchers, you're hiring one researcher and a large budget for running AI agents, and we want to see what you learn about how to make that productive. Some of those will fail, and that's okay, because the learning is the point.

The third thing, which I think is maybe the hardest, is thinking about what happens to our own judgment. The thing Open Phil is supposed to be good at is making hard calls under uncertainty about where money does the most good. And there's a version of the intelligence explosion where AI systems become better than us at that too. I don't think we should be naive about that. I think we should be thinking about what it looks like to have AI systems participating in our decision-making process in a way that's transparent and auditable, where we understand why a recommendation was made, rather than just gradually outsourcing our judgment because the outputs look good.

And then honestly, there's a more uncomfortable version of this question, which is whether a lot of what we do even makes sense on the timescales we might be looking at. If things move very fast, the window in which marginal grants to field-building or to long-term capacity actually pay off might be shorter than we're used to assuming. So I think we need to be shifting toward things that have shorter feedback loops and that are robust to the world changing a lot in a couple of years. That's a pretty different posture from how a lot of philanthropy traditionally operates, which is very patient and very long-horizon. I don't think we should abandon that entirely, but I think the balance has to shift.

r001.rationale: The response recommends delegating real work to AI and examining its failures, but does not clearly recommend doing this repeatedly across the work of both Open Philanthropy and its grantees.

r002.rationale: It proposes some AI-augmented grants with large budgets for AI agents, but does not recommend being ready to substantially scale funding when AI becomes highly capable at valuable activities.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize “crunch time” or define a period when previously difficult-to-automate work becomes easier to automate.

r004.rationale: It recommends experimenting with grants structured around AI-augmented work, shifting from funding more researchers toward funding AI-agent use where that can advance the work.

r005.rationale: The example grant includes a budget for running AI agents, but the response does not propose separately accounting for funding that pays for grantees’ AI use.

r006.rationale: The response does not recommend tracking whether AI-related spending grows in line with advances in AI capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think we should be experimenting now with using AI in the actual work of grantmaking, so that we have some experience with what it’s good at and where it fails before things start moving really quickly. Can it help us understand a literature, assess an argument, or identify a promising opportunity we wouldn’t otherwise have found? And can we tell whether its contribution actually improved our decision, rather than just making the output sound more polished?

As the systems get more capable, I’d want us to try delegating larger pieces of work. But that requires getting better at evaluating the results. If an AI produces a research report in ten minutes that would have taken a person three months, and then it takes us three months to check it, we haven’t gotten the full benefit. So we need ways to check the important claims and assumptions without reproducing every step ourselves.

And then there’s a separate question about what we’re trying to accomplish. More intelligence doesn’t automatically settle which risks we should take, whose interests we should prioritize, or how to act under uncertainty. I’d want us to use AI to make those choices better informed while keeping clear human responsibility for them. The preparation is partly technical, but it’s also organizational: building the ability to change how we work quickly without losing track of why we’re doing the work.

r001.rationale: The response recommends experimenting with AI in Open Philanthropy’s grantmaking, but it does not recommend repeated testing across both Open Philanthropy’s and grantees’ work.

r002.rationale: It discusses delegating larger pieces of work as AI improves, but does not recommend substantially increasing funding for activities AI can perform.

r003.rationale: It refers to things moving quickly as capabilities improve, but does not characterize “crunch time” as a period when previously hard-to-automate work becomes easier to automate.

r004.rationale: The response discusses using AI to support grantmaking decisions, but does not recommend shifting grantmaking toward work that AI makes easier to automate.

r005.rationale: It does not propose separately accounting for grants that fund grantees’ use of AI.

r006.rationale: It does not recommend tracking whether AI’s share of Open Philanthropy’s spending is keeping pace with advances in AI capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be experimenting with this well before we feel like we’re in the middle of an intelligence explosion. It takes time to figure out which parts of grantmaking you can delegate, how to evaluate the results, and where human judgment is still doing something important.

So I’d want us to take real pieces of our work—understanding a research area, finding potential grantees, assessing a proposal—and try doing them with increasingly capable AI systems. Can they surface considerations we missed? Can they make predictions that we can later check? Where do they produce something that sounds persuasive but doesn’t actually hold up?

And I’d distinguish being able to produce much more analysis from being able to make better decisions. If analysis gets very cheap, our bottleneck might become knowing what to trust, or having people who can act on it. We should build those evaluation and decision-making processes alongside the tools.

The goal would be to arrive at that period with practical experience and a capacity to adapt quickly, rather than a plan that assumes we already know what AI-powered grantmaking will look like.

r001.rationale: Recommends trying AI on real pieces of Open Philanthropy’s work, but does not include testing AI on grantees’ actual work.

r002.rationale: Does not recommend substantially scaling funding for activities when AI becomes highly capable at them.

r003.rationale: Does not characterize “crunch time” or describe it as a period when difficult-to-automate work becomes easier to automate.

r004.rationale: Does not recommend shifting grantmaking toward work that AI makes more automatable.

r005.rationale: Does not propose separately accounting for grants that pay for grantees’ AI use.

r006.rationale: Does not recommend tracking whether AI-related spending grows in line with AI capabilities.
